TURAL DISTRICTS.

Ma. CARDWELL is trying to get the Army
into an efficient condition. Mr. GOSCIIEN is
labouring for a like object in relation to the
Navy; whilst Earl Gualrvlnt, aided by the
Cabinet, is doing what he can to Settle the
matters now in dispute between England and
America. Mr. FORSTER is tinkering at educa-
tion and getting hopelessly bemucldleci in his
work, whilst Mr. BRUCE, what between
pnblicans' licences and bills of pains and
penalties for pooeant trades unionists, must
have more, than mortal patience if he does not
occasionally swear in the midst of the difficul-
ties by which-he is beset: The only men who
.seem free from care or anxiety of any kind are
those members of Parliament who crow like
cooks, bray like asses, bark like dogs, or grunt
like swine, when their enemies in the House
excite their displeasure by the utterance of
language disagreeable to their ears. •

Hitherto these gentlemen have regarded the
duties of the House of Commons as mere'
holiday Work. They came from their "castles
and halls" to London leaving tranquillity and
contentment behind 'them, to help in the re-
pression of extreme ideas, to shut up "Holes
in the Wall," and do other necessary work for
the safety of society. And now all of a sudden
they find out that the agricultural labourers
have become stricken by the plague of trades-
unionism, are forming themselves into societies,
subscribing and striking; and in other
ways following the example set by town
Workers with the view of raising wages and
otherwise improving the condition of their
-
class.

The ease need not be over-stated for the
purpose of effect. It is impossible to regard
the combinations going on amongst the farm
labourers in Oxfordshire, Warwickshire, and
Other of our agricultural districts without
serious apprehensions as to what may follow.
More particularly for the reason that it is
impossible to believe that our nobility and
gentry, even when aided by the clergy, can
meet 'moll an exigency with necessary gene-
rosity and wisdom, or, in fact, with any
disposition to make such sacrifices as the
necessities of the labourers' position demand.
Those labourers coming together under the
pressure of most galling wants, stimulated by
the rough eloquence of mon of their own
order, feeling at every moment of their
lives the actual evils by which they are
afilicted—eold, hunger, squalor—in youth, in
manhood, in old age; without, hope at any
time in this world, need no fanciful appeals to
their feelings. The simplest and most direct lan-
guage, the nakedest and plainest truth,derives an
overwhelming force from their common suffering.
And if ,this agitation now commencing should
Pios out of its present °dulness into the heat

of excitement, accompanied by the angry

It is but the plainest truth to say that the
worker in our fields has been most shamefully
neglected. His condition ha,s been inquired
into by Parliamentary commissions, and the
most shocking revelations have been. made
during these inquiries. Some feeble Parlia-
mentary talk has been now and then indulged
in. Philanthropists, when , the savages of
the Pacific, or the negroes of Africa have
palled on the public appetite, have now and
then made languid reference to them; but no
vigorous effort has ever been made .to grapple
with this most important of all our national
evils. The condition of the agricultural
labourer has been what it is for centuries.
Everything has changed throughout England,
whilst the tiller of the soil has remained.
the same. Ho has not had the power to
help himself, and
,nobody else has
.felt
the disposition to help him. At last,
light from the outer world is break-
ing in upon him. His partial intercourse
with his town neighbours, and his
limited. acquaintance with the cheap.
press, are enabling, him to take stock
of his position. Whilst doing this he cannot
but see that he has been
,nogleoted, left in
heathen 'ignorance, and in worse than savage
squalor and want; and if he moves at all, as
he is sure to do, now that his eyes are begin-
ning to open, terms must be made, with him
with the View to a considerable improvement
in his position, or he
,may take his affairs into,
his own hands in a most inconvenient fashion.

These remarks
,are more than justified by
the reports of meetings held in Oxfordshire
last week, where the speakers were all of them
agricultural labourers, tnd where the speeches
went in the ,most direct manner to the very
heart of the subject in hand, At one of these
meetings, held at Afollington, a labourer spoke of
his class seeing a better day, and compared what
they had to go through daily, with the better
hope that lighted their, future. Another labour-
ing orator said that "the country, socially and
commercially, was progressing, and every
class of men in it seemed to make headway
except the agricultural labourers, who were
an oppressed and, down-trodden race of men."
Warming in his argument, the same speaker
carried it home convincingly to his hearers
by fads familiar, to them all. "Now, what
was 12s. a week for a,man, his wife, and a
family of four children? Allowing a penny
a meal for each for seven days, would take
los. 6d. out of the 125., leaving Is, 6d.
for other necessaries of life." , This ealcu-
lation was followed by loud ones of
" Shame ; " and well it might ;—and loud and
ringing cheers followed the question based on
this statement:—" In a country like this,
which stood almost foremost amongst the
nations of the earth—a country that boasted
of its science, its arts, its literature and its
wealth—where every other class wore partici-
pating in the general improvements, were
the agricultural labourers, who were the pro-
ducers of food, to be served like this?
Those quotations are made almost at random,
and from amongst much of the same kind. and
of equal force, by men who are the sufferers in
the state of things complained of. And it is
fair.to ask whether landlords and farmers are
prepared with a reply. It will not do for the
gentlemen who fill the seats of the House of

Commons to go down to the country to crow at
them, or to bray, or to bark, or to grunt. The
speech of the labourers is articulate speech,
and has a very plain meaning in it—a meaning
too, as serious as it is plain. Can it be replied
to articulately by those interested on the other
side? If it can, the sooner the answer is pre-
pared the better, presuming there is any form
of logic that can be a satisfactory reply to such
a case as the labourers have made out.

The farmers, we are informed, are dis-
charging the union men and turning them out
of their cottages. The country gentle-
men, countenanced and aided by the clergy,
have pronounced the movement "im-
moral." This is just what might have
been expected,. The complaint is met
by increasing the oppression, and justifying
the tyranny by abuse. Seeing that the clergy-
man has a hand in the matter, the wonder is
it is not declared "Atheistical." There
is no handier or more eifactual epithet when
personal injury. As . oonteinplated. And who
can be an " Atheist." in the agrienituxal
districts, if the man is not one who wants to
got 16s, a week for his labour instead. of 125.?
Or how can the justice be reasonably ques-
tioned of turning the wife and, children of
such a dangerous person oup of : the- poor
cottage in which they, 4nd shelter, if society
is to be preserved? 4„

If any word we can say could have any
effect on the landowners and farmers, we
should ask them to face this difficulty in quite
a different fashion. The wages of the labourer
must be advanced, and they should in reason
and fairness advance them. The general,
condition of our agricultural population raiet
be improved, and landowners and farmers
should set earnestly about improving it. The
peace of the agricultural districts is at risk
through this movement, however it may be
conducted, and they should address themselves
to the work of preserving it. The labourer's
statement as to the improvement of all classes
but his own is absolutely true. And so is his
further declaration that his wages are not
sufficient to keep decent life in his body.
This cannot be denied. No man with any
sense of,shame, would for a moment think of
denyink it. „And now with these evils
existing, and with a growing impatience on the
part of those who suffer them, we are about to
have education added through a pressure not
put on by these poor fellows themselves, and
which when it begins to take effect must lead
to desirable changes or drive thorn, through a
sense of their sufferings and degradation, into
the madness of a headlong and blind
revolt.

The hndlords and farmers must not for a
moment suppose that their labourers will be
left to fight this battle out by themselves.
There are millions of men in England who
sympathise with them, and will help them.
Men who will insist on knowing the reason
why those whe till the fields of wealthy
England—

-hunger for such diet
As the rich man in his riot,
Casts to the fat dogs that ho
Surfeiting beneath his eye.

Men who will endeavour to see justice done,
and who will aid the labourers not only in
making their olaims understood, but in enforc-
ing them on those whose duty it is to meet
them.

Nobody in Englemd desires a revival of the
demands of JACK CIDE ; the labourers of

Btollington do not .want ..to have seven half-
penny loaves sold, for a penny; nor the three-
hooped. pots to have ten hoops; nor do they
wish to make the drinking of small beer
felony; but they do .wish to obtain for their
labour something approaching to a fair remu-
neration; something sufficient to put some
slight degree of comfort and independence
into their lives ; and it will bo a contraven-

The Memorial of the undersigned respectfully
sheweth—

" That the Act framed last session called the
Pedlars' Act, 1871, is oppressive, opposed to the
spirit of nglish. Constitutional liberty, and pro-
ductive of bad moral results." _

"A person under this Act having once obtained
the required certificate from the Police' permitting
him to carry on the vocation of a Pedlar, within a
certain district, is obliged, on travelling to another
district, to have that certificate endorsed by the
police, and in order to obtain that endorsation is
required anew to bring proofs as to his quali-

oppressiveexpense and delay. Further, in the
event of refusal or delay in granting the required
certificate, although the pettier is permitted to
appeal to ak court of summary jurisdiction, yet
inasmuch as he is not allowed to practise his
calling while the endorsement is still unobtained,

loss while the suit is pending."
"Your memorialists further desire to point out
that. a system of vast and minute police super-
vision over persons who are not criminals, is
entirely opposed to the spirit of English Cons-
titutional liberty; it tends to give a quasi-criminal
character to a lawful calling, or to bring suspicion
of criminality on respectable persons, who are
poor and helpless; and on this point your
memorialists desire particularly to call your
attention to the grave dangers attending the
spread of such a system, and the introduction of
police interference with innocent persons in a
variety of forms, a species of tyranny from which
this country has happily been free till very recent
times, and to the absence of which in this country
eminent foreign statesmen have attributed the
great respect with which English people have, as
a whole, up to the pre.sont time, regarded law,
and their readiness to assist its execution, while at
the sante time they have dep!ored the
co,ntrary. atata of matters in other countries
wnere the system which your memorialists
deprecate is in force. In connection with which
your memorialists beg to call your attention to the
growing hatred and suspicion evinced by the
poorer and more helpless part of our population

ing powers with which the Government is con-
tinually investing thire the lowest portion of the
executive.

to any one "selling, or offering for este his skill

struck at the liberty of labour, and a step is taken
towards the introduction of the mischievous
French system of workmens' "here es."

calling of a pedlar who is under seventeen years
of age, and thus by depriving many youths of
both sexes of their only chance of earning an
honest livelihood tends to drive them into reckless-
ness and crime.

that you will use your best endeavours to obtftin
the repeal of the Pedlars' Act, 1871,' and for the
discouragement of all legislation which gives
vague extensive and undue powers to the police
especially in connection with vaguely or inade-
quately defined offences.

lance Association for the Defence of Personal
Rights.

seriously advise the gentleman, who so distin-
guished. himself by imitating the crowing of
a cook—thereby producing much amusement
amongst our enlightened legislators—to make
application to the managers of our leading
music halls, where he might exercise his
talents before a not less numerous but possibly
more critical audience. It is quite refresh-
ing to me as a working man to notice the
admirable examples that are daily being shown
me. by my betters, and it is a great consolation
, to me also to notice that although my com-
peers may Sometithes storm and hiss and. howl
at an unpopular orator, that I find. a
suflicient excuse afforded. me for so doing in the
example shown me by the members of the
most. enlightened, &c., &c. It is not long since

that the new SPEAKER was introduced into the
chair of the. House of Commons amidst the
congratulations and the very eloquent adula-
tions of some Of) the leading. members of
at least one side of the House; how he

has fulfilled the expectations of his friends
has been shown by his very remarkable failure
to keep his unruly followers in order. There
is no doubt that the, scene in the House on
the 19th inst. has done much to convince us
that however unqualified our legislators are
by intelligence, to meet our, just demands,
they are determined, by means however
unscrupulous, to shelve inquiry. Jobbery
and corruption have had another lease,
but the time will most assuredly come, and
that soon, when those successes and snug
pensions which have been bestowed upon
people whose chief merit consists in their
being the descendants of loose women of the
, court of an abandoned ago, shall be completely
, swept away before the rising indignation of
an indignant people. No doubt the young
gentlemen of forty or thereabouts, and whose
ago should have taught them better, were con-
cerned in howling down any attempt to
abolish or even to inquire into the
_existence
of emoluments probably , enjoyed by their
relations; but SLR CHARLES Duda: may
congratulate himself up6n, the fact that the
House of Commons is not the British nation,
and that an appeal to the bar of public
opinion on his part will meet with a
ready response from the majority of
his countrymen. The Duke of ARGYLL, when
defending one of Mr, GLA.DSTONE'S nice little

jobs, talked in a solemn, puggish way about
appealing to the bar of public opinion to de-
fend what was justly termed a nefarious trans-
action. It was a good thing for his GRACE
that he was not compelled to court that
opinion, or it is possible that a reply might
have been given would might have somewhat
disturbed his complacency, and shown him that
the Ministry, of which he is a member, does
not command the confidence of the productive
classes. It is the duty. of every working man
to resent the gross insult that has been put
upon their representatives in Parliament.
This must not be done by noisy clamour, but
by a steady and stern resolve to obtain, by the
strong force of unitel opinion, that which
has been so temperately asked for by
the honourable Member for Chelsea. Sir
CHARLES DILKE is simply a man before his
time, and is subject to the treatment from the
bigoted portion of the community which all
such men have invariably received. Not
long since Mr. JOHN BRIGHT was denounced.
by that .press which now fawns upon him, as
an unscrupulous agitator. Insinuations of the
worst possible character were freely levelled
against him, and he was described in the pages
of our leading comio periodical as one who
was endeavouring to set class against class,
and endeavouring to instil grievances into the
minds of the working classes which did not
exist; but by the force of intellect, aided by
the goodness of his cause, he has survived the
rabid attacks of his detractors, and has lived
down the opposition which at one time
threatened to overwhelm him. Sir CHARLES
DILNE's ease will, we think, be an identical
one. In years to come he will be looked
upon by a grateful people as one who made
the first step, and was the pioneer of a move-
ment which must, in the natural course of
things, become universal. Lot all working men
combine to give him their support by all fair
and constitutional moans, and let us show that
although our betters are content to evade a
question by uttering indecent noises, we are •
content to trust to argument and sound prin-
ciple. There is no lack of loyalty to
the QUEEN amongst the multitude, but it is a
fact, patent to any man of the meanest under-
standing, that abuses exist which could be
removed without any inconvenience to her
MAJESTY. It is a false step in polities that
the inquiry asked for by Sir CHARLES DILKE
was not granted, and it clearly proves that the
House of Commons, as at present consti-
tuted, does not comprehend the just and rea-
sonable requirements of the people.

INT. H. DANIS.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of the London

receive the report of the Trade Committee on the
present aspect of affairs in connection with the
Compositors' Memorial, and to consider the pro-
priety of raising tempoxarily the amount of
subscription. The large hall was crowded. ?1t
It. Lee occupied the chair.
Mr. Self, the Secretary, read the report of the
Committee, which stated in detail what had been
done. They reported that the fifty-four hours as
the week's work was becoming an accepted fact,
as well as the advance of one halfpenny per one
thousand: 120 firms had. given in their adhesion
to these terms; but difficulties still remained with
regard to certain firms, which it would require all
their energies and determination to overcome-
Twenty-four houses stood out, and these were
what were known as piece houses ; their objeotion
was as to the advance of one halfpenny per thou-
sand. The notices would expire on Saturday, end
as the Society were resolved to fight this question

sinking details on which they differed success wae

Slll,—At the meeting of the above lodge on
Saturday last, the circular issued from the agricul-
tural labourers of Warwickshire received the
attention of the members, and it was resolved that
they render them all the support they can in their
struggle. And they consider that the time is now
arrived for every unionist in the United Kingdom
to do their duty, and give help to those who have
never yet been in a position to help themselves;
and hope that penny subscriptions will be started
in our factories and workshops, and show by that
means the numbers that consider it time that our
brother workmen are released from slavery, and
allowed to establish unions to better their condition.
From the circular we are made aware that
stringent resolutions have been passed by tho land-
owners in the district, signed by Sir Charles
Mordaunt, and posted in the villiages, as a threat
to the men, and there is not a doubt that they will
carry their object, and crush the men, if we do not
send them substantial support. Now, unionists,
do your duty; support your long neglected brother
workmen and let capital know that you intend that
the agricultural labourer shall obtain a divorce from
serfdom. Please receive 10s., from Lodge; Con-
tingent Fund 14s. 10d., subscribed by members and
friends at Lodge House.
JOHN MITCHLEY, Secretary.

LABOURERS.
At a meeting of the London Trades Council,
held at the George, Inn, Blackfriars, on Saturday',
31r. Canham called attention to the strika of tbe
agricultural labourers in Warwickshire, and the
probable movement that would take pine° for a gene*
ral rise of wages among the agricultural labourers
throughout the country. Their wages had, be said,

been systematically kept down to starvation point, so
that they were doubtless the most poor and helpless
class. He therefore considered it to be the duty
of the working classes throughout the country to
at once come to the rescue and • assist the agri-
cultural labourers. There was no class so down-
trodden, and he believed that the artisan class in
helping them would be helping themselves. The
agriculturists were frequently so poor that they
flocked to the towns, and not only glutted but
generally underworked the town labourers. If
the artisans, how Ever, could help the labourers to
got higher wages, the labourers would have more
to spend in purchasing m mufactured articles, and
the general cominunity would become better off.
He gave notice that he should move that a special
meeting be called to consider how the London
Trades Council can best aid the agricultural
labourers to better their condition, and gain an
advance of wages; and also tbat this society shall
call on the working classes to asgist the agri-
cultural labourers in their endeavours. After
several other speakers had addressed the meeting,
it was resolved that the subject should be con-
sidered at the next meeting.

YORK.
TILE BUILDING TRADES.

The strike of the masons and joiners still con-
tinues. The bricklayers have resumed work,
having accepted the conditions their employers
offered, viz., fifty-three hours in sum•ner instead
of fifty-six per week. The same concessions to
time was granted to the labourers, with a small
increase in wages, which now amounts to
19s. lOid. or Sid. more than they received the
same period in former years. They are paid at
the rate of 4id. per hour, and having made an
application to their employers to be paid 4141-d. per
hour in summer and sd. in winter, to commence
on the let of May, which would raise their wages
to Li is. per week, a meeting of the builders was
held on Wednesday evening to consider the
application, and, after some discussion, it was
resolved unanimously not to increase the labourers'
Wages. At the same meeting a fixed determind-
tion was expressed not to make any further con-
cession to either the masons or joiners.

articles.text:
WARWICKSHIRE.

THE STRIKE OF FARM LABOURERS.

The Hon. Auberon Herbert, M.P., has consented
to act upon the committee formed at Leamington
for procuring relief for the agricultural labourers
now on strike. Ho telegraphed :—" I will act
on your committee and receive subscriptions, I
11/11 heart and soul with you, and will help in every
way possible."
• The strike) was the chief topic, of conversation
at the Warwick Corn Exchange on Saturday,
when the faraiars unanimously expressed a deter-
.
ruination. not to employ any man connected with
the union. The farmers say the men are in deep
distress already, and that they complain that the
union has not afforded that assistance which was

Promised. Thera are now over 300 men on strike.
Friday evening a large open-air meeting was held
at Kineton, which was addrzased by several labour-
ing men, at the close of which a:, branch union
was formed for that district. This makee about
a dozen and a half district unions now established
in the county.. There were 231 men on the
books, but about thirty of that number had found
employment.
Sir Charles Mordaunt, through his agent, Mr.
P. Cobbe, has served notices upon all his" union"
tenants to give up possession of their cottages at
Walton and Wellesbourne ; and, if he does not
soon alter his Mind, the committee must find the
men and their families habitations somewhere to
save them from the workhouse. Other employers
have adopted the same procedure.
_ _

On Saturday the unionists obtained a great
triumph. Over 400 had been under notice to
quit their situations, and many their cottages,
bat the farmers, thinking "discretion the better
part of valour;" rescinded (in effect) the resolu-
tions against the Union, and keep the men on at
the desired adiPanee of 45., -making Ms. in many
cases. Half of those on strike have got employ-
ment at the advanced price. Professors. Fawcett
(12, Bessboro'-gardens) and E. S. Beesley (London
University), Mr. Auberon Herbert, M.P. (Old
Brompton), and Mr. F.Wilson (34, Berriers-street),
will gladly receive subscriptions for the relief of
the poor down-trodden men who have "struck"
because Sir Charles Mordaunt and his neighbours
will not give them snore than 12s. a week. The
Hon. and Rev. W. Leigh, the Rev. E. Ander-
son, and the Rev. Mr. Hobart (Rector of Welles-
bourne, the teat of the disturbance), are en-
deavouring to effect a reconciliation at an advance
of 3s.

The inauguration of the Union—now numbering
nearly 24 branches and 2,000 members—took place
O Glood Friday at Leamington.

TILE JOURNEYMEN TAIL ORS.

The tailors in this district are a gitating for a
revised"log," or aninerease in their scale of wages.
Several communications have passed between the
Masters' Association and the 'men; and the fol-
lowing letter was forwarded to the journeymen on
Saturday:—
To the Journeymen Tailors of Manchester :—ln
presenting you with the answer of the masters to
the request of the journeymen tailors of Man-
cheater for an advance in their wages, we wish
briefly to put before you the nature of that request
and the reasons that have influenced us in the
decision we have arrived at. At our first inter-
view you informed us that considerable dissatis-
faction was felt with the present time log. Nu-
merous items were pointed out requiring altera-
tion,' and a request was made that it should, be
revised by a joint committee of masters and men,
and finally that an advance of 20 per coat. on the
rate of wages should be given. These propositions
were laid before a general meeting of the masters
and fully and fairly discussed. In the face of the
keen competition with which we have to contend,
it was felt that the advance asked for was
more than could be granted; but a proposal to
meet you half-way by giving 10 percent. on the
wages was adopted. This offer was laid before
you, with the information that we were unable to
alter the time log in any way, without consent of
the various towns which were parties to drawing up
the original. Your reply was to the effect that the
advance Of 10 per cent. would be accepted, but
that you still requested the revision of the time
log by a joint committee ; and you expressed your
belief that the other towns would agred to any
alterations we might adopt. You will remember
that on two former occasions, at your request, we
appointed a committee of masters to prepare a bill
jointly with an equal number of workmen ; that
much time was given to it, and great care and
labour expended to dojustieu to both parties; and
that, although the decision arrived at was signed
by your representatives, it was on each occasion
repudiated by your Society. Under these circum-
stances we must have declined to enter a third
time into such a work had we not been prevented,
as we are, by our engagement as members of
the Provincial Masters' Association. Whilst
declining to enter into what we believe would
be a fruitless effort, we are quite willing
to consider, and to amend, if necessary,
any part of the bill that the experience of the last
four years has shown to require , it. With this
view a meeting of the Provincial Masters' Ass°.
eiation was called in this town. Seale improve-
ments were ,suggeste,l, which w3re to be referred.
to the various branches for confirmation. We now
beg to hand you the results, and feel sure that
when you have. carefully perused them you will
admit that your 'employers have not been un-
mindful of your interests. To obviate a fruitful
source of difference between employers and their
workpeoplo, a Committee of three masters has
been appointed, to.unite with an equal number of
workmen to be appointed by you, as an Arbitra-
tion Committee to settle any dispute that may
arise as to the description of material. We now
offer you the log of 1868, as revised, with the ad-
vance of ten per cent. on the rate of wages which
you have already approved.—l am, on behalf of
the Manchester Master Tailors' Assooiation,
yours truly,
Wturs.sx B. Heywoon, Hon, Sec.

articles.title: OUR AGRICULTURAL LABOURER'S.
articles.text:
OUR AGRICULTURAL LABOURER'S.

Owners of land have had their incomes increased
by the general increase of the industrial activity
of the country. Manufacturers and merchants
have become fabulously rich through the same
cause. Professional men, in like manner, have
had their incomes greatly increased. Nay, even
the men who toil in the workshops and faetories&
the country have had their hours of labour shortened,
their wages inereased, and in many ways, by
means of their trades unions, have forced from
their employers some increasi, however inadequate,
in their weekly incomes. -
Why is it, we may ask, that the agricultural
labourer has not been a partaker in this general
progress? Why is it, that however long his hours
of toil, or however enterprising his, epirit, there
is no hope that be can rise in the social scale?
From early childhood constant, unvarying drudgery,
is his doorq, The seasons follow each other, with
their varyillt beauties anti their crowning . abun-
dance, but it is his fate only to work, and never
to enjoy in fulness that teeming wealth the ekist-
en3e of Which is due in great part to his labour.
Now we say that to breed men had women
for labour, only is to degrade them below the
condition of brute beasts. To shut them out from
all chance of participation in the comforts and
advantages of civilisation—to leave them witkont
even hope in connection with the struggles of
life, is to inflict on them the deepest injuries
which men, even in a savage and heathen state,
can inflict on each other.

That it is the duty of the, agricultural labourers
to bestir themselves to put an end to such a state
of things, who can doubt ? or who can for a
moment hesitate in declaring that every man,
whatever or wherever his employment, who lives
by his labour, ought to lend his aid in promoting
any well.considered movement the agricultural
labourers may set on foot for the improvement of
their condition?

What is the use of political reform to the
workers in our fields? Of what advantage to;
them is the progress of civilisation or the growth
of national wealth P To work whilst they are able,
and to become parish paupers when ago takes the
strength out of their limbs, is all the privilege
that civilisation, religion, and wealth have given
them, and until they themselves protest ener-
getically against it, nothing elso will be done for
them.

That things are wrong nobody can doubt. How
to put them right is a matter more difficult to
pronounce upon. Better wages is a natural first
step, ,and ought to be taken without further delay.
Better houses must also be procured. Education for
their children will no doubt soon be universally
insisted on. But more must be done. Every
labourer ought to have land attached to his cot.
tage, and if he is skilful and industrious, he
should have the opportunity of increasing the
quantity of his land on such conditions as may
enable him to rise to the conditiOn of a comfort-
able small farmer.

A groat deal has been written against small
farms; and rich people and crottheity economists
have declared over and over again that extensive
scientific farming is better calculated to increase
the riches of the nation. We are sure. the argu-
ments they use are quite capable of refutation.
That refutation, however, 'is not now called for.
To grow rich is not the first business of life for
individuals or nations. To become happy, moral,
and wise, are far higher and more ennobling aims.
We have as a nation grown richer than any,
other nation in the world now, or at any past
period—but we have, in the misery of our agri-
cultural labourers, a great source of national
weakness, a standing obstacle to our national pro-
gress.
The attention of the nation and the attention
of Parliament must be directed to this; we have
been reforming all sorts of things, and we must
now reform. the state of affairs in our agrieal.
tural districts. We must make comfort and
happiness possible for this large and most im-
portant, class or our peciple, and we are pleased
beyond measure that the labourers are bestirring
themselves. They will get help of the best kind
m i
,fro their follow working men n the towns and
cities of the kingdom, and by prudent and peaceful
action, in time, this Standing disgrace to our
rulers—this misery, ignorance, . and squalor in
connection with the condition of the agricultural
labourer, will be banished from thii land.—The

THE CITY,

On Monday afternoon a public meeting was
held at the 'Mansion House to promote the
establishment of an industrial school for the
City of London, in connection with the
National Refuges for Homeless and Destitute
Children. The Lord Mayor presided, and
there was a numerous and influential
attendance.
After Mr. W. Williams, the secretary of the
committee of the National Refuges, had read a
statement showing the results which attended
the training of the children who had been
taken from the streets and placed either in the
Chichester training ship, the Farm School,
or the Refuge in Great Queen-street, Holborn,
Sheriff Sir John Bennett moved: "That one
chief means of preventing the increase of
crime, vagrancy, and pauperism is to rescue
neglected children—large numbers of whom
find their way into the streets to bet?, or steal
—and to educate and train them ill industrial
pursuits for a useful life."
Mr. Walter, M.P., seconded the resolution.
The motion was :supported by Mr. Botley,
and adopted.

"That the objects contemplated by the City
of London Industrial School for Boys; namely,
the rescuing of orphan, neglected, and aban-
doned children from a street life, and giving
them a sound, Christian education, combined
with industrial training, are eminently
calculated to diminish vagrancy and crime,
and to convert the 'human material,' now
running to waste, into useful and honourable
men; and, therefore, deserves the hearty
support of the citizens of London.''
Alderman Sir R. W. Carden seconded the
reposition.-
The resolution was adopted, and a list .of
subscriptions was read, including contributions
of 50 guineas from Mr. John Sands, .E 25 from
Mr, Walter, M.P., and £2l from Mr.
Peek, M.P.
Mr. Fitzwilliam then- proposed, and Mr.

LONDON SOROOL BOARD.

ELECTION FOR WESTMINSTER
FELL° w ItArneAvEns,—l have been invited again to
offer myself as a candidate for a seat at the London School
Board now vacant in the Westminster Division.
The Education Act has not been a success. It has led
to theological and denominational discussions, rather than
to united and intelligent efforts on behalf of National
Education. This has convinced me that all causes of dis-
sension should, as far as possible, be removed; and as
what is called the religious difficulty, is the main obstacle
in the way of practical educational work, I consider that
in any system of National Education, the State should
make provision solely for the secular instruction which
all children may receive in common ; and that the respon-
sibility of the religious teaching of the young should ho
thrown upon. the various religious bodies.
The Act was passed to provide a good and useful secular
education for every boy and girl in England. No school
was to receive a farthing of public money unless conducted
on principles entirely unseetarian. The sending of child-
ren within certain ages to school was to be, by degrees at
least, compulsory; and, to this end, the schooling was to
be gratuitous in the case of those whose parents were
without means of paying for it.
Iliul the Act been carried out in thii spirit by the Lon-
don School Board, the education of the children of working
men would not have been delayed, and the bitterness of
feeling now existing among religious parties would have
been narrowed. r

As the question of the payment of Denominational Fees
is yet undecided by the Board, it is important for those
who are against this system to avail themselves of the
present vacancy, and secure the return of a candidate who
18 against it. . . .

It' is agreed that, in a question concerning the interest
of the people,, they should be represented by some men
from among themselves, and I, therefore, offer myself in a
district to which, by long residence, I belong, and for
which there is reason to believe thit I should have been
elected in November, 15714 had proper arrangements been
made for taking the votes.
Relying on your support for ultimate success,
I am, yours obediently,
GEORGE POTTER.
P.B.—Meetings, at which my views will be more fully
explained, will be held throughout the district previous to
the day of election, which is fixed for Patumr, Aran

articles.text:
WORKING MEN'S COMMITTEE
FOR PROUOTING THE

SEPARATION OF CHURCH AND STATE.

TO TILE WORKING CLASSES OF GREAT BRITAIN.

FELLOW WORKMEN,-

The Working Men's Committee has been formed
in consequence of a prevalent impression that
the time is come when the question of Separa-
tion of Church and State must be referred to the
final judgment of the people. In the last Session
of Parliament, it was submitted by Mr. Mien to
the judgment of the House of Commons. In
doing this, he had no expectation of immediate
success. As, however, an Act of Parliament had
separated the Church from the State in Ireland, he
felt himself warranted in asking the Legislature t )
apply the principle of that measure to the . cat of
the United .Kingdom. He was met with the cbjee-
tion that the case of Ireland was peculiar—wnich
indepd it was circumstantially, but not substan-
tially. Nevertheless, the Government which had
undertaken the disendowment and disestablishment
of the State-Church in Ireland, did not oppose the
motion upon its merits, but attempted to show that
the question was not yet ripe for legislative action.
Mr. Gladstone closed his speech by suggesting to
Mr. Misfl, that he must first convince a majority
of the people of the wisdom and justice of his
policy, before expecting Parliament to adept it. ,
This unequivocal challenge of the Premier has
been accepted ; and the Society for the liberation
of Religion from State-Patronage and Control has
determined to appeal to the people for an expres-
sion of opinion on the subject. The Working Men
of 'Great Britain have never yet, as a body, pro.
nounced any judgment on this great question; but
it has been felt that, afterthe broad challenge thrown
down by the Premier, they can no longer, with
respect either to him or to themselves, refrain from
a declaration of their honest and deliberate senti-
ments. From Mr. Miall, and the great party that
he has formed in the country, Mr. Gladstone, as
leader of the Liberal party in the House of Com-
mons, and also as first Minister of the Crown, has,
in set terms, appealed to the People. It behoves
Working Men, therefore, to answer that appeal;
and that, not simply upon the purely numerical
ground suggested by Mr. Gladstone as to whether,
among the adult population of this Island, the
majority are in favour' of, or against, the Dis-
endowment and Disostablishment of the• State-
Church in Britain, as in Ireland ;% but also,
and perhaps -especially, with a view to the
return •of pledged candidates at the next
General Election, whensoever that may take
place. The House of Commons, as now consti-
tuted, does not embody a feithfal and com-
plete representation of the whole people; and,
without taking a poll of the whole population, the
only means of answering the challenge of the Pre-
mier consists in the election of a House of Cominons,
each member of which has been returned with a
special view to his avowed opinion on the great
question thus gravely put to the issue.
These then, are the circumstances under which
the Working Men's Committee for promoting the
Separation of Church and State has been formed,
and now proceeds to work.
The views of the Committee may be thus con-
sisely stated-
1. They regard matters of religion as belonging
to the domain of oonsoience, in which everything
must be left between man and his Maker.
2. They are of opinion that, since the State
Church in one part of the United Kingdom has
been disestablished, it is both unjust and incon-
sistent not to deal in a similar manner with the
State-Churches of the other parts of the 'United
Kingdom
3. They aro persuaded from observation and
experience, that the State-Church has utterly
failed to acoomplish tho task for whick it was
established; and are also convinced that its
existence, as such, is a fatal hindrance to the
attainment of those objects which churches of any
kind profess to keep in view.
4. The State-Church of England has failed as
manifestly as the State-Church in Ireland; the
only difference being, that, while the bulk of the
Irish People were Roman Catholics, in contradis-
tinction to the avowed *Protestantism of the then
State-Church, the great majority of the British
People are either members of the different Pro-
testant Nonconforraist Churches, or of the Church
of Rome, or are willing to remain of no Church,
rather than attach themselves to the Establish-
ment.

The immense revenues Of the English and
Scottish Establislunents alone constitute a great
argument against their continuance ; because
those revenues, though the common property
of the whole nation. are distributed among the
religious teachers of half, or less than half, of the'
people. Enormous and disproportionate salaries
and emoluments are paid to Bishops and other
Diritaries, while, of that portion of the fund
which is received by the parochial clergy, by far
the largest part falls to those who have the fem cat
parishioners, and the smallest to such as minister
among the densest populations. •
6. The obstructiveness of the Establishment is
an additional reason for abolishing it. Its bishops
and clergy are neither appointed nor controlled by,
nor are they respoosible to, the People. Jealous
of their own privileges, they resist all changes
which may affeet their own ascendancy, or that of
the Establishment in which they have so strong a
vested interest. Hence, in every agitation of a
political or social character, they are always on
one side and the People on tie bther.

THE BUDGET.

Mit. LOIVE'S Budget this year is more for-
tunate than last, though neither satisfactory to
the true financial reformer nor affording much
cause for rejoicing to the bulk of the people.
A pretty large surplus not merely liberated
him from the unlucky task of inventing some
new tax, but enabled him to reduce somewhat
the burden of taxation, if not to make any
positive and entire repeal. It remains, how-
ever, for Mr. JOHN BRIGHT, or rather for that
party of retrenchers at which he hinted as
necessary for the purpose, to accomplish those
measures of sweeping economy whereby alone
full justice can be done to our overweighted
cauntry and people.

The Chancellor of the EXCUEQUER had
a great deal to say on his improved me-
thod of making the estimates; but the only
way that would greatly interest the whole
public would be one " which should
leave out of the reckoning some ten
or twenty millions of lavish and
needless expenditure that might be well
spared under a truly wise and frugal Adminis-
tration. The same remark mu' s to the
genuinely patriotic, mind, when Mr. LowE
expresses his desire that the whole expendi-
ture of the year shall be defrayed within the
year, Nations and States, like individuals,
ought to live within their annual income ;
but the great 'thing is for States and nations
to subsist politically upon the smallest income
that will answer the end instead of doing as we
have so long done, screwing all the money that
could be screwed out of the taxpayer, and
apologising for the wasteful and oppressive
extortion by referring to that wonderfully
powerful constitution which enables JOUN' Bum-.

still to stand upright in his top-boots after
all this bloodletting. It may not bo possible
, under every contingency todo without supple-
mentary Estimates, but it ought to be very
possible, and must be made practicable, to
effoot very big reductions in the principal
Estimates for the financial year.
Even Mr. LOWE, however, hopes to go on

diminishing the National Debt, and is able to

point to the Navy as the only department of the
public service in which, instead of an increase
of expenditure beyond estimate, there has not
been a decrease, and in several instances of
considerable amount. In the Civil Service,

for instance, he boasts of a saving of upwards

of half a million; but then he does not state
his total as an ultimate fact. Nothing, in

reality, can be well relied upon but the upshot
of the whole account, from which it appears,
that the Minister begins the next financial
year with a surplus of £2,815,000 at his dis-
posal, of which £2,220,000 represents the
falling of actual outlay below prospective
estimates. The one thing which, after all,
stares us in the face is, that the Government
of the country for the year now closing, has
cost us the enormous and shameful sum of
£71,720,000.

As to economy in comparison with that fine
thing "elasticity of revenue," it appears that
of the whole surplus, somewhat over a million
is due to saving in expense, and the remainder
amounting to,not much under two millions, to
mere increase of revenue. With regard to the
future, Mr. LOWE .has not much to offer in the
Way of reduced estimates. The old Muse
still plays its part. If the country is to be
defended by the very best means, ho does not
cc how "any one can say that the Estimates

are unreasonably extravagant." Perhaps
they may pass for this year, and a year or
two after; but let would-be statesmen roly
upon it that the time comes steadily on when
those only will be able to maintain themselves
in power who can give us hope of providing
amply for •every real financial necessity by
two-thirds, or one-half the amount of money
paid in yearly taxation.

articles.title: WARWICKSHIRE LABOURERS.
articles.text:
THE WARWICKSHIRE LABOURERS.

Tut: strike of the agricultural labourers in
Warwickshire, under any view of it an in-
teresting feature of the times, seems not un-
likely to assume something like national pro-
portions of importance. In fact, to those who
have the best opportunities of j udging, matters
look as though a conflict were imminent be.
twixt the farmers and the labourers generally.
We cannot wonder that the rural tenantry
should take the alarm at the application of
trade union principles to the relations in which
they and Those on whose handiwork the field
work depends stand towards each other as
classes. If they reflect, however, they will
perceive that there neither is nor ought to be
any escape for them from the tendency of
labour, in all its kinds, to claim its due, and
to assert and indicate its rights. When, too,
they bear in mind the changed attitude of the
working hands towards the introduction and in-
crease of mechanical apparatus in the processes
of the farm, they ought, if not from thankful-
ness yet in an intelligent spirit of self-defence,
to meet the improved conduct of the peasantry
by a behaviour towards them showing proper
appreciation of this great moral change, and
adapted to encourage, and oven reward, its
fullest and constant manifestation.

That the farmers should deprecate and dread
a general strike at a season of the year when
they most require the steady and contented
labour of industrious hands, is very natural.
And no doubt it were much to be desired for
the sake of both parties and of the public in-
terests at stake, that so inconVenient, expen-
sive, and unsatisfactory an experiment should
bo averted. Whose fault, however, is it that
the labourers are come to feel themselves
under a necessity of having recourse to this
extreme and illogical argument? .What a
strange feature in 'human • nature it is, that
neither iudiVidual men, nor whole classes of
them, can ever be persuaded to profit by
the experience of others before them, but
must learn from bitter experience of their
own, and, even then, are slow and unwilling
to learn those simple truths which all ex-
perience in every ago and nation uniformly
teaches! Here arc Warwickshire farmers, a
county which comprises such towns as Bir-
mingham, and Coventry, apparently reckoning
that they have nothing to do but discharge all
hands who join the Labourers' Union, when
they cannot but know, unless they remain as
ignorant and unthinking as the clods of their
holdings, that not those 'groat emporia alone,
but every manufacturing town and district in
the whole kingdom has been constrained to
acknowledge the folly and vanity Of encoun-
tering the spirit of Trade Unionism with
execration and resistance.

Now, at any rate, these forms of association,
combination, and co-operation, have obtained
recognition, sanction, and protection from
Parliament. And, consistently • with that
concession, the eleetorial vote has been
widely extended among the working
classes; so widely as to make inevitable its
ultimate and not long delayed extension to
every male of full age, paupers, criminals, and
lunatics excepted. Instead, however, of
taking these things into consideration, the
farmers seem to he cherishing the hope that
between the seedtime and the harvest they
may be able to dispense with the services of
the Unionists, and drive them to the necessity
of returning to work under unimproved con-
ditions, or, at best, of accepting a mere frac-
tion of what they reasonably demand. Nay,
no increase is held out to any but those who
entitle themselves to it by refraining from
joining the Union. As if such a boon would
extract from five hundred men as much work
as was before got through by twice or thrice
the number.

Everybody knowo that, from any savings of
their own, the farm labeurers aro not prepared

to stand out for over, or even for any long
time. Common sense, nevertheless, tells us
that men, women, and children cannot be
allowed to starve; and to starvation there are
no alternatives, for the farmers at least, but
support for the breadless out of the poor's rate
or so large a migration from one district to
another, from agrieultural to manufacturing
districts, as may too much denude the fields
of the hands needful for their profitable tilth.
If the farmers be wise, not to say liberal, they
will follow the same reasonable example of
Lord LEfan, who has offered fifteen shillings
in answer to the demand for sixteen, rather
than push matters to an outrance, by which
they might punish the men and their families
much, but themselves much more.

articles.title: SCHOOL BOARD ELECTIONS.
articles.text:
SCHOOL BOARD ELECTIONS.

THE London School Board does not seem to
have many attractions for those who succeeded
in getting themselves placed on it. Already
Lord L.twitENcE, occupying the chairmanship,
has shown his anxiety to get away, and has
only consented to remain on conditions whieli
relieve him from the heavy work which no
doubt overtasked his strength. Mr. HUXLEY,
TORRENS, Dr. MILLER, Lord SANDON, and
Mr. ROGERS have absolutely got clean off; and
we are now in the midst of contests for their
successors.

It would be well if we could get at the exact
cause of this disinclination to • remain on the
London Board. One reason, and perhaps the
principal one, is that the work is heavy
and without remuneration of any kind,
and in saying this we wish to in-
sinuate nothing mercenary against the
members of the Board ; on the contrary,
we consider it unfair to expect a continued
performance of public duties without some
kind of payment, or at least some hope of it,
as a sweetener of labour. That the labourer is
Worthy of his hire there can The no question.
And the members of the School Board who
have been working bard, though they have
done little, are no exception to this most
wholesome rule.

Another probable reason for these' raiigna-,
tions is perhaps the disinclination of lima Of
ability to sit week after week for the purpose
of discussing questions of almost purely
denominational interest questions worn
quite thread-bare by never-ending, stilt.
beginning discussions of tlke most dreary
round-towel kind—questions which never can
be separated from men's prejudices, and which
are therefore incapable of settlement by right
reason or common sense. There may be
sanguine persons who thi4 such discussions
do goad; but people of sense and experience
cannot regard them otherwise than with
hopelessness of heart. If any one thing in
this world, but death, can be certain, it is
that the. spirit of sectarian controversy will
never die out; that wherever a chance of
growth is given it will flourish; and that
wherever it flourishes it will interfere with the
growth of all honest desire to unite men for
necessary common objects. This was said
before any of the School Boards were elected,
and it may be repeated now, backed by over-
whelming proof, to be found in the twaddlinge
and contentions of these Boards.

Have the electors learned anything front
this? If they have not, they should at once
see if they eau study the lessons it teaches.
The children are yet without school accom-
modation. Tho country in general is without
a definite practical plan of instruction. Op
posing factious trot out their candidates when
an. opportunity occurs, and the terms"
"bigot," and "godless," fly about with as
Much vitality as ever. When is this mis-
chievous game to end? When will our people
have sense enough to turn a deaf ear to such.
discreditable nonsense? We really want men
on the School Board who will not allow educa-
tion to be delayed by these sickening sec-
tarian contentions ; and who, when the
schools are opened, will not have the so much
needed instruction of our poor children de-
layed by religious brawls. To talk of religious
teaching in schools which form a battle-ground
for rival sects, is to talk of an impossible thing.
The very soul of religion is peace, goodwill,
and
.unity of spirit. And if the ministers of
our yarious nets were placed iu the schools as

masters to teach, carrying with them a spirit
of proselytism, which, in the very nature of
things would be a necessity, instead of a
religious education we should have an educa-
tion of strife and division worse in its effect
on the moral conduct of the scholars than a
well ordered Heathenism.
Let us, therefore, have, front such sew elec-
tions as may take plain), men who know the
requirements of the children of the poor, and
who will insist on a sound early education
for them; men who feel that the lower classes
cannot be lifted till by education the
power is conferred on them to . raise
themselves; men who are not eneinies to re-
ligion, but who will not allow the rivalries
of sects to stand in the way of necessary moral
and intellectual training for the poor. A little
more manliness of thought and action on the
part of our voters would soon settle this ques-
tion. At no very distant day it must be
settled, the present position of affairs being
too disgraceful to continue. A few dozen
working wen on the Boards would be a great
help. Middle and upper class people, perhaps,
seeing this refuse in any number to vote for
them. And even working men lack that zeal
which, if it existed in anything like proportion
to the need for it, might carry the true friends
of liberal education over all difficulties. We
hope the contests now on will show us there
is an improvement in this respect, as it is most
desirable that working men should not eon-
sciously play the game of those who seek to
neutralise all agencies operating for the true
improvement of the condition of the masses.

THE NONCONFORIIISTS AND THE
EDUCATION ACT.

The Central Nonconformist Committee have
issued a circular, in which they say :—"We Must
show that the Country is more desirous of securing ,
religious equality for the sake alike of education
and religion than her Majesty's Ministers suppose.
Our organisation must be more complete and our
policy more active. Public action is forced upon
us, and we, must dot shrink tom accepting its
responsibilities. A Nonconformist committee
should be organised in every village and town, and

THE TAX-PAYERS AND COXSTIrVENCIES

INSULTED.

In the recent discussion on the Army Estimates,
the representatives of Birmingham, .Warrington,
dtud other largo towns, speaking ia the interests of

their heavily burdened constituents, urged a re.
duction in the enormous expenditure of the army,
whereupon the Member for Chelsea, Sir IL
Hoare, uttered the taunting observation that
"those honourable Members cared more for the
wishes of their constituents than for the honour of
their. country." This taunt elicited loud cheers
from many Members who are interested, for
various reasons, in maintaining a high and un-
restrained expenditure of the public money. But
it certainly appears most unwarrantable to in-
sinuate that the constituencies, who have to pro •
vide the present extreme t txation, are less com-
petent judges of " the honour of the country" than
those who, either personally or through their
relatives, are in many instances largely benefited
by the distribution of the money so raised. In the
present co,ndition of Prance, the old bugbear of
a French invasion, which was so long the pretext
for increasing armaments, cannot be urged, even
by the most determined panic-monger. Mr. Muntz
said, in the discussion first alluded tO, that the
idea of future armed interference on the Continent
must be given up as absurd, in the face of the
enormous armed hosts mint Lined by those
nations, with the number of whose soldiers this
country can never pretend to compete. The
people of this country have rad for their arma-
ments since the Peace of 1816, snore, than a thou-
sand millions of money, and now because, through
some of their representatives in the House of
Commons, they are protesting against the enor-
mous sum of £18,500,000 (including the cost of
barracks) demanded of them this year for the land
forces alone, they are to be told in their own
House of Parliament that they don't care any-
about the honour of their country. Well, at any
rate, it is hoped they will bear this taunt in mind
at the next election.

Tuittp-cLAss RAILWAY TICKETS.

A very desirable innovation in railway manage-
ment is spreading so rapidly that we may. antici-
pate its becoming universal. The Midland
Company having proclaimed its adoption of the
policy of running third-class carriages by all
trains, the North Staffordshire quickly followed
suit. An official announcement states that on and
after ilia Ist of April all the trains of the London
and North-Western will convey third-class pas-
sengers with the exception 9f the Irish and Scotch
Limited Mails and the suburban trains running in
connection with the North London lino. The
Manchester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Company
also announce that on and after April 1 they will
issue third-class tickets over ail parts of their line,
by all trains. The introduction of the new system
is happily titnad to give the public the advantage
of it in Easter week. Its adoption throughout
the country will confer a boon not easily to be
oyer-rated, upon the poorer classes of
.society.
Not only will their oPpertunities of going about be
multiplied; but there will be an end to the practice
of compelling them to choose between travelling
at inconvenient hours of the day arid paying
the higher fares. It is reasonably to be expected
that the stimulus imparted to locomotion by this
liberality will make the change as advantageous
to the railway companies as to their customers.

articles.text:
THE SUPERIORITY OF ENGLISHMEN.

After the late war in France, a good deal was
said and written about the hardihood of the
Prussian troops, until at last an opinion got
abroad that they were as superior to ottr men in
stamina as they were in training. This was a very
obvions fallacy to all who had had opportunities
of seeing both under similar circumstanees. As a
proof that in physical capacity the Englishman is
superior to the Gorman, I may mon tion a fact

which appears in the German papers. A great ;
number of men from the north of Prussia we!li
some time ago to Newcastle to replace the Eng.
lish labourers who had struck work. These, it
appears, are all returning, worn oat and emir
Mated, having, by their own account, been
utterly unable to perform the work demanded of
them in England. It may be said that this DJ an
isolated instance. I have, however, been repeatedly
assured by Germans who have resided in America, •
and had men of all countries in their employ, that
there is a vitality in the Englishman which is noi
to be found in the men of any other nation.

MR. MIINDELLA ON THE PATENT LAWS-
On Monday, in a Committee of the House of
Commons sitting on Letters Patent, Mr. llun•
della, M.P., gave evidence. Be said te had'been
connected with a trade for '25 years wadi bad
been in a transition process, and 25 years ago
the whole of that manufacture was by hand;
but to-day nine-tenths of it was by power-loon).
He believed every invention that bad conferred
value upon trade had been the subject of patent.
Although no longer actively connected with 410
business with which he was connected so long, ho
might say that for 23 years he took out in England
fully 25 patents, nearly as many in France and
Germany, and some in America; but the patents
which they took out abroad were always in relation
to the power of the foreigner to come and compete
with them. During the whole of •this time they,
had never infringed any patent. Some of these
patents had created quite a revolution in the trade;
and, in every instance they were the invention
of either overlookers, or workmen, or working
mechanics. He should have no difficulty in
showing. the Committee that every invention
that had been successful had conferred benefit
upon the inventor and upon the public; and he
should show that every invention that had not
been :successful had only incurred loss upon the
patentee. Mr. Mundella then went on to support
this proposition. lie was distinctly in favour of
granting patents; and if these were abolished he
was certain that inventors, who were a very small
body, would take their patents where there was A
patent law. He would not grant dog-in-the-
manger or unworkable patents; and ho would
compel every patentee to work his patent within
a certain time or forfeit it. The hon. member than
related how their firm invariably took a man by
the hand to perfect his invention, and gave him
one-third of the proceeds of his invention.
