always open to the inhabitants of Hamburg,
who had always considered them almost as
public property. The orders given are in the
meantime being carried out, and there will
soon remain nothing of that delightful pro-
menade.

Several Cornish tin Miners have been en-
gaged by the young Khig of Siam to develop
the, gold deposits in his dominions,

There is soniething touelling in the inge-
nuity displayed in dunning their delinquent
debtors which tradesmen grown 'desperate
sometimes display. Thus a hardware mer-
chant in Knoxville, Tennessee, declares in an
advertisement that "a hardware business can
no more be carried on everlastingly without
money, than a dog can wag his tail when he
hag none." "My customers," adds the suf-
ferer, "are all good, but what good does a
man's goodness do when he don't do any
good ?" A question which numbers of persons
may well ponder seriously.

On the 24th the body of a woman was found
in the Queen's Park, Edinburgh. It was also
naked, and• from the appearance it presented it
is conjectured that the woman must have met
her death by foul play, as her head was
slightly out, and her body bruised in iratiolli
parts. Her clothing was found lying about.
No cluo has been obtained by the police as to
the assailant, and the body had not been iden-
tified. The woman appears to be about forty
years of ago. The case is being investigated
by the police.

An °facial order, signed by Mr. H. A.
Bruce, the Secretary of State, has been issued,
abolishing the fair known as "Horn Fair,"
held annually at Charlton, on the 18th of
October and two following days, and also the
fairs held for the sale of pigs, horses &c., at
Blackheath, on the 13th May and horses,
Oc-
tober.

An affray took place on the 23rd at Neath,
ariring out of the jealousy of the Welsh
colliers against the Englishmen employed. in
the mines. Twelve or fourteen waylaid four
or five Englishmen on their way hoe, and a
terrible affray. ensued. Three mon were
stabbed, and one of the Englishmen was
beaten until his features were undistinguish-
able. Several men are in custody.

On the 25th, according to custom, her
Majesty's bounty was distributed at the Lord.
High Almoner's Moe, Whitehall, to the
blind. and aged. The recipients varied in age
from•6o to 80 years, and received from live to
ten shillings each. .Yosterday the Maundy
money and clothing was distributed. in the
Royal Chapel of Whitehall. ,

The London and North Western, the Great
Western, the Great Northern, the Manchester,
Sheffield, and Lincolnshire, and the Lancashire
and Yorkshire Railway Companies have de-
cided to commence attaching third-class
carriages to all their trains, and that return
tickets between London and Manchester and
other places in the north will be available by
any et the routes.

A lamentable and fatal accident with a
paraffin lamp took place at Bermondsey on the
night of the 23rd. A woman named Tyler
loft three of' her young children in her kitchen
while she went upstairs. In their play they
overturned a large paraffin lamp, which set fire
one of them, a boy about nine years of age,
who was so much burned that he died on the
following night.

Owing to the disturbance which took place
on the 20th at the Paris School Of Medicine, the
following notice was posted up an Sunday on
the walls. of the building wine time before M.
Dolbeau was to commence his lecture In
consequence of the disorders produced on-
March 20,- the faculty has unanimously decided
that medical pupils shall be admitted. to the
amphitheatre on the presentation of their
cards of inscription; awl that if any riot is
renewed the leatures and examinations will
he suspended." :About 300 Or 40 'idlers
assembled in the open space in front Of the
building,, with about 30 or 40 Police-agents,
but curiosity seemed to be. the only motive
of their 'remaining. No demonstration took
plea() outside, but Within the building the
learned professor was frequently interrupted,
and at last obliged. to desist.

The clergymen of Sheffield and its neigh-
bourhood have addressed an important
memorial to the Archbishop of York. They
state that the two Convocations of York and
Canterbury do not represent the Clergy of the
Church or the nation, and they recommend that
a national representative body shall be con-
stituted of which the bishops should be ex
officio members and the rest of its members
appointed by. efection ; the clerical members
to be elected by the clergy, and the lay
members by the laity; they express their
confident belief that under a eouncil so con-
stituted the Church would surmount her
troubles for the time is gone by when ie
might rely dl
on the dignity which privilege and
antiquity. confer. The memorial has excited
much interest in Yorkshire.,

At. a meeting of professional and amateur
Milsiciens, held at the College of Organists
recently, it Was, aetermined to invite. Mr.
Goss to a public banquet at the Albion on
April 17th, on which occasion Mr. W. H.
Uladstene, M.P., will take the chair. In con-
sideration of the long and useful service ren-
dered by the veteran composer to musical art,
it has been proposed to raise a fund for the
purpose of endowing a musical scholarship,
oz. presenting some suitable testimonial to him
Oil his official retirement from St. Paul's
CathoJral.

On Monday the Royal Geographical Sooiety
bold its seoond meeting for the present month,
at the London University, under the ohair-
manship of Sir Henry Ravdinson. Mr.
W. G. Palgrave, who about five years ago
wawa valuable contributor to the society, rata
a highly interesting paper, detailing a journey
made by him during his late resident:3e as.
Consul in Asia Minor. At the conclusion of
his lecture Mr. Palgrave was warmly ap-
plauded, and, at the suggestion of the chair-
man, received a cordial vote of thanks.

Her Majesty's birthday will be kept on
Saturday, Juno 1,• instead of Wednesday,
May 13, as previously announced.

Lady Charles Innes 'Caritas so far recovered
from the effects of the late accident in the
hunting field as to bear the fatigue of removsl
to her town residence at Rutland-Kate.

• A constable of the Irish constabulary, named
Trail, has mysteriously disappeared from
Limerick, where he had been ordered on duty
to the assizes. As his sword is also missing,
and the locality of Killarney having been one
of the disturbed districts during the Fenian
rising, it is feared he has been murdered by
some notorious member of the confederation.
No clue can be ascertained of his fate.

On the 22nd the brig, Viscount Lambton, of
Rochester (Beck, master), went ashore on
Yarmouth beach. The surf lifeboat Duff,
belonging to the National Lifeboat Institution,
was fortunately enabled to save the whole of
the crew from the wreck. The brig Ark, of
West Ilartlepool (Dick, master), afterwards
went on the Barber Sands. The crew were
landed at Caister at three o'clock in the morn-
ing, and subsequently the master returned to
his vessel with the Caister henchmen, and
ultimately they succeeded in getting the
brig into Yarmouth harbour in a very leaky
state.

The mails from Kiel to Copenhagen have to
be conveyed
,over the land portion of the
distance by coach instead of train from Korsor,
on account of the heavy snowfall, 'which has
rendered railway communication impracti-
cable.

The Geological Museum of the University
of Rome has just received as a present from
King Victor Emmanuel, a magnificent collec-
tion of Peruvian antiquities, comprising a
number of silver vases, some extremely
curious musical instruments, a coloured gar-
ment made from the bark of trees, and some
arrows and lances. These last are notched,
ornamented with feathers, and have wooden
heads, showing that they belong to the period
when the use of iron, was unknown. The
whole of those articles were found in a bed of
guano, and evidently date from the earliest
antiquity.

On the 23rd, at the Bradford Police-court,
two men, named George Hanson and Alfred
Jager, both from Carlisle, were charged with
having assaulted a man named Craven on the
11th of January, and robbed him of £5 Os. 11d.
The prisoners were remanded.

According to the annual poor rate return for
the year ended Lady Day, 1871, the total popu-
lation of England and Wales was 22,70,1,108.
During the year £7,886,742 had been ex-
pended for relief of the poor as against
£7,644,307 in the previous year, making a
difference of 3.2 per cent.

Energetic efforts are now being made by the
Vie toria-park,Prepprvation Committee to secure
the land adjeiniag ,Hackney-common, which„
in the course of a few months, will pass into•
the hands of the Metropolitan Board of Works,
and with this view the honorary secpetaries of
the .Soeiety have applied to the Baroness.
Burdett Coutta to induce that lady try pur.
chase the comparatively small strip of land,
some four or live acres, between the park, and
the common, the whole to be thrown open as
a recreation ground for the people.

At a meeting of students, held on the 25th,
to consider the present rectorial contest
of St. Andrew's University, the Marquis
of Salisbury was formally withdrawn by
the proposer, who recommended the sup-
porters of the Marquis to vote for Lord
Neaves. Sir Round°ll Palmer and the Dean
of Westminster were duly nominated and
seconded. The &lens of the respective can-
didates were set forth at length by their sup-
porters, after which the meeting broke up,
amid much uproar..

The Allan Company's steamer Nestorian,
which proceeded .to Queenstown on Tuesday,
contained, among 500 passengers, about 160
who are going to the United States, to make a
new experiment in emigration, viz., to found a
colony in the State of Nebraska composed
entirely of Englishmen.

A special meeting of the Birmingham Anti-
Income Tax Association was held on Tuesday
to consider the Budget introduced by the
Chancellor of the Exchequer. On the motion
of Mr. Bennett, seconded by Mr. Pardon, it
was resolved—" That, while approving .the
reductions lathe Income Tax proposed by her
Majesty's Government, and especially of the
increase of the abatement allowed on small in-
comes and its extension to incomes of £3OO
per annum, this Committee is of opinion that
nothing but the entire abolition of schedule D
can be accepted as a satisfactory settlement of
the question."

A. loan of eighteen millions of francs has
been sanctionel by the Dlunicipal Council of
Paris for the erection of schools in that
capital.

A Paris Correspondent says that X. Thiers
has withdrawn his protootton from Marshal
Bazaino, and that the latter is to be tried by
Court-martial in acoordanoe with tho recom-
mendation of the Committee a Inquiry into
the Capitulations. .

The trial of William Chester Minor for the
murder of George Merritt in the Belvedere-
road, Lambeth, will take place at the Kingston
Assizes on -Thursday, April 4. Mr. Denman,
Q.C., is the leading [counsel for the prose-
cution.

On Tuesday, at the Leeds assizes, Ediard
Brooke, a manufacturer of Bradford, was con-
victed of having forged a bill of exchange for
£2,000 upon a local bank, and was sentenced
to seven years' penal servitude.

Last week the aggregate mortality in London
and twenty other largo towns of the United
Kingdom was at the rate of 25 deaths annually
to every 1,000 persons estimated to be living.
In the metropolis 2,103 births and 1,463
deaths were registered, the former having
been 274 and the latter 224 below the average.
Forty-eight persons died from small-pox, 66
from measles, 19 from scarlet fever, 6 from
diphtheria, 102 from whooping-cough, 31 from
different forms of fever (of which 7 were cer-
tified as typhus, 19 as enterio or typhoid, and
5 as simple continued fever), and. 15 from
diarrhoea. The mean temperature was above
the average on the two first days of the week,
thus raising the warm period which com-
menoed on the 12th of December last to 97
days, during which the temperature was, with
but a few exceptions, continually above the
average; the daily excess in these 97 days
was 5.1 degrees. Cold weather set in on
Tuesday, and on each of the last five days of
the week a considerable deficiency of tempera-
ture was shown; Thursday was the coldest
day, when the mean was only 30.3 degrees,
and 12 degrees below the average.

By a Majority of 118 votes against 9, the
Bavarian*Chamber has refused to sanction a
grant of 20,000 florins, asked for by the
Government as a subsidy to the ministerial
papers. The Premier had previously an-
nounced that even if the grant were refused,
the Government would find means of duly
representing its views in the press, and ask
afterwards for a Bill of Indemnity.

• According to the daily weather report, the
barometer has again fallen on nearly all the
coasts from which returns are received, and
there has been much snow in the north and
east of the kingdom.

A petition presented by one of the creditors
of Sir W. Russell, M.P. for IsTelwich, asking
for a certificate to the Speaker of the House of
Commons, declaring that the hon. baronet had
not carried out the terms of a liquidation, was
on Tuesday before M. Registrar Roche, who
dismissed the application with costs.

The Claimant to the Tichborne baronetcy
has addressed a letter to the Daily News, in
which he appeals to the public for subscrip-
tions to enable him to carry on his defence.
While describing the charges against him as
"foul and groundless," he points out., that
they will involve the whole question of his
identity, and states that six counsel, including
the Attorney-General, Mr. itawkins, Q.C., and
Serjeant Parry, have been retained for the
prosecution. The Claimant describes himself
as utterly penniless, declares that he has been
cruelly persecuted, positively asserts that he is
Sir Roger Tichborne, and expresses his confi-
dence that the British public will see that
justice is done by securing him a fair trial.

At Bow-street on Tuesday, a firework
manufacturer, of Goldsmiths'-row, Hackney,
was fined £2O for having carried on his busi-
ness without a licence and within 50 yards of
a dwelling-house. His stock was also
forfeited.

A rumour is eiroulating in Paris that the
immediate evacuation of the French depart-
ments by the German troops is likely to take
plaoe at an early day. France is to pay
Prussia a sum of fire hundred millions of
franca at once, and the rest of the indemnity
by instalments.

Another candidate has come forward for
the vacancy in the Greenwich division of the
London School Board, in the person of Mr.
Henry Gover. He advocates the reading of
the Bible in the schools, "a hearty co-opera-
tion in the work, without regard to the differ-
ence of religious views, no abuse of the Act
for party or sectarian purposes, no use of the
schools as religious battle-fields, no concurrent
endowment, technical instruction to be given,
opposition to all extravagant outlay, and
practical and energetic action, with a view to
the earliest possible results."

The Court of Aldermen have resolved to
present a vote of thanks to Colonel Fraser,
the Commissioner of the City police, for the
admirable arrangements made by him on the
occasion of the Thanksgiving Service at St.
Paul's.

It is stated that the Sultan of Turkey has
announced his intention of paying a visit in
May to the Exhibition whiela is to be hold at
Lyons during the present season.

The Exchequer receipts show that up .to
Saturday last, when 51 weeks of the financial
year had elapsed, the revenue amounted to
£73,297,871, an increase of nearly a million
sterling over the Budget estimate for the
whole twelvemonths. The expenditure had
been £68,718,792. The balance in the Bank
of England is £9,774,962.

As the Army Estimates show a reduction of
£50,000 for wages in the Laboratory Depart-
ment of Woolwich Arsenal, there is a current
report at Woolwich that 400 workmen are to
be immediately disoharged from the Govern-
ment establishments in that town.

--
We learn from Berlin that the Empenr of
Gbrmany is now quite restored to health.

From Brussels we have intelligence of a
boiler explosion at a woollen manufactory
there, by which it is feared eight persons have
been killed, and many others injured.

A Correspondent at Cherbourg sends an BC'
count of the arrival there of the Queen on Sun-
day afternoon. It seems that when the State
railway carriages were sent from Paris for the
use of her Majesty they were hissed and
hooted as they passed through the outskirts of
the city, on the supposition, apparently, that
they had belonged to the Emperor Napoleon.
As a measure of precaution naval gendarmes
and policemen were stationed on the bridges
and at the level crossings of the single line
which leads from the private station in the
Arsenal to the main line to Paris. Into that
station no strangers were admitted. As the
Royal train left Cherbourg there were a few
shouts of "Vire la Reine," but the people
generally seemed to feel, the Correspondent
says, that the best way of showing respect to
their visitor was to respect the privaoy under
which she was travelling.

At the Liverpool Assizes, the woman •
Poulton, who had been found guilty of
stealing a child three years ago, belonging to
Mrs. Council, of Liverpool, was sentenced to
seven years' penal servitude.

A Gaffing gun, proposed to be mounted on
the backs of camels for use in India is in
course of trial by a select committee at, Wool-
wich. It has ten barrels, each 42. inch bore,
and is sufficiently light to be fired from
tripod fixed on the back of the camel without
inconvenience.

The Empress of Germany has sent the fol-
lowing very interesting letter to the
Director of the Evangelical Protestant
Deaconesses' Institution at Tottenham Green,
together with the Cross of Merit for Women:
"In this late war—now, through the help
of our Lord, gloriously ended—for the inde-
pendency and fame of Germany, have the
Deaconesses, and especially the Sisters of the
Sisterhood directed by you, worked with all
that devotedness that is in accordance with
their noble calling, and have comforted and
done good to many a wounded and sick
soldier, as well on the place of war as in
Germany. His Majesty the Emperor and
King deeply acknowledged these services of
true Christian humility done at home and on
the seat of war under most difficult oircum-
stances great sacrifices, and self-denial. To
acknowledge these services to each Sister
separately by giving her the Cross of Merit
for Women would not be in accordance with
the spirit and principles which induce the
individuals to give their services for love te
their Lord and Saviour to the benefit of the
whole Sisterhood. The gratitude towards
them for their noble services, however, is not
in the least diminished by that. To oxpreeo
this to you and *your Sisterhood with.
whole heart gives special satisfaction to Iner
and I herewith ask you to assure each ono
personally of my sincere gratitude. Accord-
ing to the order of his Majesty the limper"
and King, I enclose for a continual retool"
brance of that which your Sisterhood has so
nobly done, the Cross of Merit for Women'
and ask you to deposit as such at your institn"
tion. May also this testimony of honour
often renew the remembrance of gratitudo
which the Empress and Queen of GermanY
felt at a time of great need for equally great
help.—(Signed), AUGUSTA."

A tragical incident occurred last Friday at
the Thatre des Varietes in Toulouse. An
actress, Madame Vert, was upon the stage
performing her part, when she suddehlY fell
upon her face and was found to be dead.
The audience, which had believed that the
actress had only fainted, was informed of the
truth, and the performance was diooll-
-

A horrible crime has just been oomm4.tt4d,
at Fombrie, a farm in the Gironde, oectipieu
by M. Mainveille. The proprietor Was
killed by his servant with an axe. ,The bloW
was given with such violence that the hailcue,.
broke short, and tho head laid. open so tilt"'
the interior was visible. The dowelled lea";
young widow and .a family. The cause°
the murder is not kilown, bat the perpetrator
15 1A custody.

The journals of Toulon state that an attempt
has just been made to poison the fathers of
the college of Sainte-Marie at La &pie, near
that port. After the evening repast some of
them were taken ill, and two days later fifteen
where in bed, while those who were not so ill
could scarcely hold themselves upright.
Suspicion fell upon one of the servants named
Joseph Deyenez, and he was arrested. A
chemical examination of the water served at
their table showed the presence of a powerful
poison. The attempt was confined to the
fathers, as none of the 280 pupils in the
schools were in any way indisposed. No
death has ensued.

Adviees from Mexioo state that Guerra
Martinez and Trevino have boon beaten by
General Rocha at Zacatecas, who is pursuing
the enemy.

Russia having granted the decoration of St.
Stanislas to Monsignor Marini, who is entwasted
with the negotiations of the appointment of
the bishops in Russia, this distinction, the
Times correspondent telegraphs, is considered
at Rome to indicate the renewal of official
relations between the Holy See and Russia.

The vacant fellowship at University College
has been filled up by the election of Mr. E. J.
Payne, 8.A., of Charsley's Private Hall. Mr.
Payne was placed in the second class by the
classical moderators in Trinity term, 1869, and
IF the first class at the final classical examina-
tion in Michaelmas term, 1871. There were
seven candidates.

Archdeacon Denison has published a corre-
spondence between himself and the Rev. H.
B. Barry, inspector of schools. The Arch-
deacon, in his letter, refuses absolutely to
admit a Government inspector within his
school. He will be happy to provide him with
luncheon, and allow him to "inspect the
schools from outside ; " but he neither has nor
will have a "conscience clause." He has
"nothing to do with the Elementary School
Act except to denounce it as irreligious." If
called upon to pay a school rate, he says he
will refuse, and the amount will have to be
levied on his property under a distress war-
rant.

A large proportion of the majority agmun
the motion of Sir C. Dilke was composed of
the Conservative party, Mr. Disraeli and most
of his colleagues on the front Opposition
bench having gone into the lobby with the
Government and their supporters. Amongst
tho. members who did not vote were Mr. Jacob
Bright, Mr. Alderman Carter, Mr. Dixon,
Professor Fawcett,. Mr. Charles Gilpin, Mr.
Illingworth, Mr. Leathern, Mr. Midi, Mr.
Morley, Mr. Osborne Morgan, Mr. Bernal
Osborne, Sir Robert Peel, Mr. E. Potter, Mr.
T. B. Potter, Mr. C. Reed, Mr. H. Richard,
and Mr. James White. The tellers for the
minority, which consisted of Mr. Anderson
and Sir Wilfrid Lawson, were Sir C. Dilke
and Mr. Auberon Herbert.

Mary Pennell, the. housekeeper of a de-
ceased solicitor, Mr. Tepper, of Notting-hill
and Bedford-row, was discharged from Lam-
beth Police-court, where she appeared on the
accusation of having stolen a gold snuff-box,
'valuable plate, and papers of her late master.
The magistrate thought the prosecution had
done wisely in withdrawing the charge, as
the prisoner, an old servant, probably believed
she was entitled to hold the property until
claimed by some legal authority.

On the 23rd, at the West Riding Assizes at
Leeds, a cloth-dresser named M'Criough was
sentenced to six mouths' imprisonment and
twenty lashes for a robbery with violence ;
and two men were sentenced to seven years'
penal servitude
.for burglary and arson at
Bradford.

PEOPLE'S GARDEN AT WILLESDEN.

gress, with a view to the opening for the season
1872 on the 4th May next. During the recess
greenhouses have been erected and some thou-
sands of plants collected. The Members.
band has also made good progress and
will prove a great attraction. The cricket
field of seven acres, croquet grounds, gymnasium,
maze, &c., are in course of completion, and every
i
arrangement s being made to render the season
1872 a groat success. The season-tickets have
been fixed for this season at five shillings, and are
in course of issue from the offices,32,Foloy-street,
Portland-place.

The Irish Times announces that the Kerry
election petition has been withdrawn.

Business will to a large extent he suspended
in London next Monday, which is one of the
four Bank holidays of the year. In addition
to the Stock Exchange, Lloyd's, the Corn
Exchange, the Fire and Life offices, and
various Mincing-lane and other firms, the
great Manchester and other wholesale houses
of the City, &e., have adopted these annual
holidays, and will close on Monday accord-
ingly.

An Italian journal, 17 Pensiero, published at
Nice, gives some information respecting M.
Emile 011ivier, about whom but little has been
heard since tne commencement of the late war
between Prance and Germany. M. 011ivier is,
it seems, residing at a village called Pollone, a
short distance from Biella, in Northern Italy,
where he lives a very retired and studious
life. He is reported to have said on a recent
occasion that he would not have accepted office
under Napoleon M. if his Majesty had not
assured him that he would not make war with-
out his consent. That consent he persistently
refused to give, until he was compelled, as it
were, by seeing that the press regarded. the
insult to the French Ambassador as a public
question. M. 011ivier says that he shall not
return to France until the Emperor Napoleon,
of whom he spoke with much emotion, is re-
called to the throne by the French themselves,
an event which M. 011ivier considers is sure to
OMIT.

Complaint is made by the Debats that the
English Government displayed more alacrity
than the Breneh Government in making public
the denunciation of the Commercial Treaty.
The very day the denunciation took place
Parliament was informed of it, and the tele-
graph conveyed the news to Paris. "It is
assuredly deplorable," adds the Debats," that
official communications in France should be so
tardy as to be, in a measure, without interest;
and that we should, for the most part, be com-
pelled to look to foreign sources for exact
information on our own affairs."

In the Turkish budget, which has just been
issued, the expenditure for the year is estimated
at 21,404,150 Evros, and the income at
20,637,210 livres, thus showing a decrease in
the former, and an increase in the latter,
compared with the figures of last year. The
Turquic makes the announcement that the
Porto intends to balance its accounts in future
without having recourse to large loans.

A Post Office notice states that after the
31st instant official post-cards will be sold
to the public in packets only—the smallest
packet containing twelve cards, and the larger
ones twenty-four, thirty-six, forty-eight, and
so on. The price of a packet of twelve cards
will be sixpence-halfpenny, and the larger
packets will be charged in the same proportion.
Single post-cards will no longer be sold.
Arrangements will shortly be made for im-
pressing with a halfpenny stamp, at the office
of Inland Revenue, post-cards other than
official post-cards, subject to certain restric-
tions.

The jury which had been engaged at 'Alp-
zie, in Trying Herren Liebkneeht, liebel, and
Hessner for high treason, has found the two
former guilty, and acquitted the latter. Her-
ron Liebk neat and Bebel are sentenced to
two years' imprisonment each in a fortress.

The official Gazette promulgates the com-
pulsory electoral law, and the financial law
for 1872. General Iforst, who has lately
directed the Cis-Leithan War Department,
has now been appointed Minister of that De-
partment.

King Victor Emmanuel left Rome on Mon-
day for Florerce. Prince Frederick Charles
has arrived at Messina from Tunis. He will
visit Catania and Syracuse.

The Indian Observer special correspondent
gives a full and circumstantial account of the
recovery of little Mary Winchester, so long in
captivity among the Looshais. Here is an
extract:—" Mary Winchester is at length

articles.title: LATEST INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
LATEST INTELLIGENCE.

THURSDAY,
Mr. Gladstone will leave London to-day for
the Easter recess.

Her Majesty the Queen will hold a Drawing
Room at Buckingham Palace in the beginning
of May, in addition to the one already
announced for the 23rd April. His Royal
Highness the Duke of Edinburgh will hold a
Levee, on Her Majesty's behalf, on Friday,
April 12. It has been found necessary to
alter the day on which her Majesty's birthday
will be kept from the 15th of May to Saturday,
June 1.

It is said that at the meeting of the
Warwickshire agricultural labourers, which is
to be held on Good Friday, an important letter
will be read, signed by Mr. Thomas Hughes,
Mr. Mundella, Lord Edmond Fitzmauriee,
Mr. Andrew Johnston, and other members of
Parliament.

The Field-Marshal Commanding-in-Chief
has bestowed a distinguished service reward of
£lOO a-year upon Colonel B. O'Brien half-pay
late Military Train. Colonel O'Brien served
during the Crimean War in the 77th Regi-
ment, including the battles of Alma and
Inkermann, and the siege and fall of Sebas-
topol; he served with the 87th Fusiliers in
the Indian Mutiny campaign of 1857.

A meeting of the Executive Committee for
Promoting the Special Loan Exhibition of.
Ancient Musical Instruments was held on
Wednesday at the South Kensington Museum.
The Duke of Edinburgh presided, and there
were present Lord Gerald Fitzgerald, Mr. IT.
Leslie, Mr. P. C. Owen, and Mr. Alan S. Colo
(secretary).

It is stated that Mr. Roby, the Secretary
of the Endowed Schools Commission, has been
appointed a member of it, in the place of Mr.
A. Hobhouse, Q.C., who was lately promoted
to be Legal Member of Council at Calcutta.
Mr. Douglas Richmond succeeds Mr. Ruby
as Secretary.

A distressing accident happened yesterday
at Shobden-court, the seat of Lord Bateman,
in Herefordshire. Maude, his lordship's
eldest daughter, seized, as its supposed, by a
fainting fit, fell into the fire, and, before as-
sistance could be given, was severely burnt on
the arm and slightly on other parts of the
body. Her state, though very painful, and
likely to remain so for a long period, is not
believed to be dangerous.

At a mooting of the Home Rule Association
held in Dublin last night, Mr. P. J. Smyth,
Professor Galbraith, Mr. A. M. Sullivan, and
Capt. King Harman, who delivered addrestes,
agreed that the movement was malting most
satisfactory progress. Professor Galbraith
declared that they would not be deterred in
advancing Home Rule by the English press
or Government.

Mr. Thomas Longman has printed three
letters which have recently been addressed to
him by Sir Charles Trevelyan respecting the
compromise offered by Canada in reference to
the reprinting of English copyright books. Sir
Charles strongly urges the adoption of the
plan advocated by the Government of Canada,
viz. :—To pay to the owners of English copy-
right an excise duty of 121 per cent., equal
to the Customs duty chargeable, but not really
levied, on the frontier, provided they were
allowed the same privilege of reprinting
English copyright works for sale out of the
United Kingdom which was exercised in the
United States. Ile submits that the circum-
stances call for early and decided action.

A telegram from Singapore announces the
loss of the ship Bombay, Captain Hughes,
while bound from Iloilo, in the Phillippine
Islands, with a full cargo of sugar to Falmouth
for orders. She was totally wrecked going
through Balabac Straits. Cargo all lost, and
crew saved. She was a ship of 937 tons,
owned by Mr. G. D. Tyser, of London. She
was built at Harwich in 1861, and was
completing a round voyage from London to
Hong-Kong, Iloilo, and back, when lost.

A fire broke out yesterday morning in the
extensive warehouses of Fraser and IPFaren,
in Buchanan and A rgyll-streets Glasgow, and
extended to the premises of id.'Ciosh, iron-
monger, and Aitken's Temperance Hotel.
With the exception of. the hotel, which is
only partially damaged, the buildings and
stock are entirely destroyed. The fire was got
under with great difficulty. The total damage
-is estimated at £lOO,OOO.

Mr. Devereux, member for Wexford
Borough, has resigned his seat on account of
ill-health. The hon. gentleman has re-
presented the constituency for seven years.
He is a Liberal and a Roman Catholic. The
election to this vacancy will not take place
till after Easter.

DUTY.
To the Editor of the BEE-HITE.

Six,—There are some men who would seem to
think that it has nothing to do with everyday
life whether there is a God or not; andthat if
there were no God they could live for self
alone, without being responsible to anyone,
provided they passively conformed to the
letter of the law.
And there are others who would seem to
think themselves justified in actively using
the law as an instrument to condemn, excom-
municate, and persecute as evil, all who do
not profess belief in some ancient stereotyped
dogma; and these practically treat morality
and belief in a God as quite secondary, and
valueless as compared with acceptance of their
authority• as infallible, and, power as
supreme.
But if there wore not a God, and " the few"
powerful and rich cared not either to .appease
the sufferings, or propitiate the favour of the
masses in order to reconcile and bring them to
be at one with themselves, why should the
mass respect the few ?
And if there were a God, who, as a loving
and merciful Father, cared for the masses' then
why should the mass respect 'the few,"
unless they acted towards the mass as such a
God would have His servants and worshippers
act towards the mass? But if the few rich
cared for the suffering mass, then such men
would be as instruments, angels, or servants of
God to the mass, and their presence would
be as the presence of God amongst the
mass, whether the poor believed in a God or not.
And such conduot of the rich towards the poor
would at least cause the poor to think the
rich believed in a God; and so this conduct
would lay a foundation for bringirg unbelievers
to believe not only that there was a God, but
that He was also loving and merciful. And
this, a true faith in God, would be founded on
a true faith in man. But when on account of
either hypocrisy, false testimony, evil deeds or
doctrines, a true faith could not be placed in
those who occupied the seats of the Scribes and
Pharisees, then this foundation for a true
faith in Goci would be destroyed, and justice
would require that the destroyers of such a
divine faith should, as false stewards, be put out
of their exalted seats. And if there were not
laws in force for the adequate redress of these
wrongs, then the masses would be provoked
andsjustitied in redressing these wrongs them-
selves with a high hand, if justice was not to
be obtained by any other means.
And since those who at present occupy the
National Churches testify against one another,
making it as impossible to believe both or
either as it was impossible to believe the testi-
mony of either of the elders in "the story of
Susannah ; " therefore the masses ought to
rise and secure a hearing in the National
Churches for those who are unjustly excluded
from addressing them on behalf of the crucified
Jesus, as the people of Israel secured a hearing
for Daniel on behalf of the accused Susannah.
And this would be the people's duty if there
were no God, but it increases their duty to do
so, when the good and merciful God they pro-
fess to believe in is falsely accused of evil and
slandered, because Bishop Dupanloup in Franco
asserts that the slanderer of a priest is as bad
us a murderer of hostages; and, therefore a
slanderer of God must be worse than either.
And whilst priests accuse God of evil (as they
do) and revile one another, the testimony of
some must be false; thou for the sake of God
and truth let the people require that the pulpits
of the National Churches shall be opened with-
out favour or fear to a free and fair discussion
of what is taught as necessary to be believed.
This is the duty of the people, because evil
doctrines are established as true and are them-
selves the cause of an immense host of evils.—
Yours, &c., -

T. G. HEADLEY.

, STATE AND CHURCH IN AMERICA.

The Executive Committee of the Society
for the Liberation of Religion from State
Patronage and Control, feeling it to be
desirable to obtain exact information respecting
the relations of the civil power in the United
States to religion and to religious bodies, and
the working of Voluntaryism in that country,
on Tuesday invited the Rev. Dr. Dexter, of
Boston, and the Rev. Dr. Healy, President of
Straight University, New Orleans, to address
a meeting at the Westminster Palace Hotel.
The second named gentleman was unable to
be present. Mr. Carvell Williams read a
letter of apology from him.

opening the meeting, referred to the absolute
separation in America of the Church from the
State, and maintained that the religious life of

times amusing description of the history of

or territorial associations, for civil government.

it Was determined in the oldendays that the

old condition of things was changed, and the

portant information, the pith of which was

Opinion that money Was a positive curse to
